overview: The file consists of a two-page U.S. Department of State list of papers concerning marine engineering and shipbuilding in Japan. Its nine entries, numbered 31–39, summarize reports and cross-references dated from 1930 to 1939 on government control and consolidation of shipbuilders, shipyard profitability and reporting restrictions, vessels under construction, Osaka Shosen Kaisha’s acquisition of Kawasaki Shipbuilding Company shares, new shipbuilding laws and finance, subsidies, and possible Japanese battleship construction. The underlying telegrams, reports, translations, and newspaper article are described but are not reproduced in the supplied text.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers on Japanese marine engineering and shipbuilding, entries 31–39
subfiles.about: An administrative index summarizes and cross-references nine papers dated 1930–1939 concerning commercial and naval shipbuilding in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Entries 31–34 cover proposed government-backed consolidation of shipbuilders, figures showing unprofitable operation at most yards, Japanese shipyards’ refusal to supply tonnage data, and a published table showing stages of ship construction. Entries 35–38 concern Osaka Shosen Kaisha’s purchase of Kawasaki Shipbuilding Company shares, translations of two 1939 shipbuilding laws, subsidies, government loans, and possible interest relief under the Shipbuilding Finance Law. Entry 39 records Naval Attaché Roll’s information about the construction of an OCR-uncertain number of battleships. Several entries direct the reader to other State Department decimal files rather than enclosing the referenced material here.

interest: The list provides a compact chronological map of American diplomatic and commercial intelligence on Japan’s shipbuilding industry during the 1930s. It is especially useful for tracing the relationship between industrial consolidation, poor commercial profitability, state subsidies and finance, increasing secrecy among shipyards, and possible naval expansion. Its cross-references also identify where related material was filed elsewhere, while the note about Kobe–Osaka yards withholding tonnage information offers evidence of growing restrictions on foreign economic intelligence.
